claims.text: The proposed starting material is a nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The initial multilayer interfaces possess stable local chemical short-range order.
The initial multilayer has minimal preexisting dislocation density.
Sustained loading concentrates stress at the FCC/BCC multilayer interfaces.
Mechanical loading can progressively disrupt local short-range order at chemically heterogeneous interfaces.
Reduction of local short-range order lowers barriers for dislocation nucleation.
Plastic deformation under sustained load is activated primarily by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation.
The proposed interfacial process promotes deformation twinning in the softer layers.
The stronger layers remain intact and continue to bear most of the applied load while the softer layers deform.
Coordinated dislocation slip and deformation twinning can distribute plastic deformation and delay localization or failure.
The coordinated plastic processes can combine high strength with substantial deformation tolerance.
Under sustained loading, the multilayer will accumulate plastic strain progressively and in a stepwise manner.
Dislocation slip and deformation twinning will be localized preferentially at the multilayer interfaces.
Sustained loading will measurably reduce interfacial short-range order relative to an unstressed control.
The coating architecture will remain intact during the proposed progressive plastic deformation.
An otherwise identical unloaded control will show negligible plastic deformation and no significant evolution of interfacial short-range order.

The proposed mechanism is restricted to isothermal loading conditions that retain the nanoscale multilayer morphology and avoid catastrophic failure, rapid layer mixing, coarsening, or immediate necking.
Failure to observe progressive strain together with localized dislocation nucleation and reduced interfacial short-range order relative to the unloaded control would falsify the hypothesis.
